@Kim Morrison thank you for this. Please note that due to earlier submissions that failed on the Palomar side with the notice "This is a fault at our end, not with your submission", my GitHub account catskillsresearch accumulated a delay penalty.

I completed a run of Mizar CCL following the bug fix, but when I attempted to submit another project, Scott 1964, I was placed on a 3-day cooldown.

Since the penalty was incurred due to a platform-side error rather than an issue with the submissions, would it be possible to reset the delay penalty for my account? I am actively collaborating with Dana Scott on these formalizations, and keeping momentum on this work is very time-sensitive for our team.

Additionally, as feedback on the current rate-limiting policy: applying an account-wide cooldown across separate repositories creates a significant bottleneck for users managing multiple distinct formalization projects under one GitHub account. It would be very helpful if the platform could consider scoping cooldowns on a per-repository or per-project basis in the future.

Thank you for your time and help.

The situation changed from 3 day timeout to "Submission intake is temporarily unavailable. This is ours to fix, not yours. Please try again in a moment. "

I am trying to submit catskillsresearch/scott1964 .

This morning it progressed back to asking if I wanted to drop a prior submission (which I did: the MizarCCL one), then it said

MizarCCL accumulated delay penalities for submissions during the period where there was an open PR to fix a blocking bug that was beyond my control.

I ran into the same thing: valid proof, but submission fails resulting in penalty delays.

I opened a PR that avoids one instance of this issue, mechanical verification failed due to OOM / resource exhaustion:

PalomarSubmission#130

As a follow up to above: it would be very useful to have larger resource levels beyond the standard one. #130 provides groundwork for that.

Big proofs currently can't be posted to Palomar because they don't verify within the allotted resource constraints. I think this includes the recent Navier Stokes results, given that nobody has published them yet: https://github.com/openai/NavierStokesAndEuler

Idea: submitters could pay to submit huge proofs given the infra costs. Maybe anything above the basic tier requires prepayment. If there's interest, I'm happy to help implement.

For example: Anthropic's Fermat formalization requires > 153 GB for lake build, 300 GB memory for Comparator.

@DC I have 6 entries in Palomar but a side-effect of runs attempted while PR#120 was pending is that I am now getting cooldown delays of "come back in 5 days" or more. As a result, in terror of getting any kind of error in a run, I have imported Palomar's process into my own githubs as a "preflight" run that I can repeat on my PC as needed using my own LLM tokens without delay. For complicated projects that are still under the 1000-line cap currently enforced, using GPT5.6, I find that I spend up to $20 in tokens (using Cursor). To not have to worry about cooldown delays, for an official registration run, since I'm paying it anyway on my local preflights, I would gladly stick the cost of the tokens for the run into Palomar with a credit card. To keep the sizing proportional to the run, you could add this charge at the end of the run (when you know how many tokens), or do what Cursor does and ask me to put in enough prepaid token budget to cover what I expect the run to consume (based on my preflight on the identical model).

I would also like to see the line caps removed under that pay-as-you-go model, so for a formalization of a paper we can put in every key theorem and definition in the paper. What I do now is cover that by validating theorems which I know depend on other theorems, so I only validate the frontier of the blueprint of the paper. However, I like that it matches the strength of the English language statement of a theorem and the Lean version. That is diagnostically very useful for double checking that the strength of the English matches exactly the strength of the Lean expression. I would like to have the ability to check more theorems in this way, not just the frontier of the blueprint.

It would be great to see Anthropic's FLT proof run through Palomar. Of the 29,500 theorems, maybe 99% are theorems that are machine generated proof fragments, with the other 1% being "name" theorems. A Palomar registration could stick to FLT itself or FLT plus the name theorems used in its proof. That doesn't scope the cost, however. Lake compiles around 60,000 files to check the proof. This can take 4 or 5 days on a single PC. A 96 core server with plenty of RAM can go faster. It is hard to imagine how to frame the context for the policy prompts to do their work. The lines of code vastly exceed any current model's context window. It would an interesting collaboration with Anthropic to figure out how to run the policy prompts effectively on a proof of that size.

hello using a phone, typing is a little awkward apologies. for anyone hitting the cost of Codex: upload git bundles over the UI, tell your AI to mock the lean/lake executables, do the work at OpenAI's expense on a standard subscription and get it to give you a git bundle back plus a shellscript you can cut/paste and run locally. this is the protocol i am running. scripts and protocols in repos below. please respect AGPLv3+ and GFDLv1.3+ licenses, thank you.

https://gitlab.com/d12rg/d12rg-hypergroup-lean

lesson learned from debian project maintenance: everyone not following the debian development protocols (in full) ends up rediscovering them, reinventing "alternatives", or everyone suffers such as "5 days to build 60,000 source files into binaries..." without asking "why can't i just get these 60,000 binaries from a standard distribution?"
that i feel is the question that should be being asked, Lars. you should be able to upload those, or collaborate with others to split and share the work. without needing to spend months reinventing the requisite infrastructure. as a FOSS developer of... 31 years, solving this one has always been on my mind.
